name: spinach ricotta pasta
instructions:
A ricotta-and-greens pasta built on seared ricotta (or food-processed cottage cheese) + food-processor-chopped greens + cream + garlic. Nutmeg and red chili flakes carry the flavor — more so than the greens themselves (see notes).

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- pasta
- olive oil
- garlic
- ricotta cheese and/or cottage cheese (see notes on the swap)
- spinach, parsley, mixed greens (or really any greens — see notes)
- heavy whipping cream (as much as needed to bring the sauce together)
- nutmeg (to taste — critical, see notes)
- red chili flakes (to taste — critical, see notes)
- cayenne pepper
- lemon juice and lemon zest (to taste)
- pasta water (reserved from cooking)
- salt, black pepper

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. Cook the pasta in well-salted water. Reserve some pasta water before draining.
2. In a separate pan, cook the garlic in olive oil until fragrant (don't brown).
3. SEAR/COOK THE RICOTTA (OR FOOD-PROCESSED COTTAGE CHEESE): add the ricotta (or cottage cheese that's been run through a food processor to smooth it out) to the garlicky oil. Let it cook against the hot pan — searing gives it a slightly toasted, more concentrated flavor rather than reading as raw cheese.
4. Chop the greens (spinach + parsley + mixed greens) in a food processor. Fold them in after the ricotta has seared.
5. Add heavy cream as necessary to bring it together into a proper sauce.
6. Season with nutmeg, red chili flakes, and cayenne — all to taste. Nutmeg and chili flakes are the load-bearing flavors here (see notes).
7. Finish with lemon juice and lemon zest to taste.
8. Add the cooked pasta and enough reserved pasta water to loosen the sauce and get it to coat the pasta.
9. Salt and black pepper to taste.
notes:
=== NUTMEG AND CHILI FLAKES ARE CRITICAL — MORE SO THAN THE GREENS ===

The greens carry visual/textural weight but the FLAVOR of this dish is nutmeg + red chili flakes. Without them the sauce reads flat and generic-creamy-cheese. With them it reads as a proper composed dish. Add both to taste — don't skimp. If you're going to under-do anything in this recipe, let it be the greens; if you're going to over-do anything, let it be the nutmeg and chili flakes.

=== SEAR/COOK THE RICOTTA — DON'T LEAVE IT RAW ===

Cooking the ricotta (or food-processed cottage cheese) against the hot garlicky pan is a real technique step, not just heating. The searing gives the cheese a slightly toasted, more concentrated flavor that reads as an actual cooked component rather than as a raw dairy dollop stirred in. Skip this and the sauce reads flat and dairy-forward without the cheese pulling its weight.

=== RICOTTA OR FOOD-PROCESSED COTTAGE CHEESE — INTERCHANGEABLE ===

Either works. Ricotta is smoother out of the tub. Cottage cheese needs a food processor pass first to smooth out the curds — unprocessed cottage cheese would give you visible grainy curds in the sauce, which reads wrong. Same swap-friendly cheese-role framing as tomato-tart's bulk cheese role.

=== GREENS — REALLY ANYTHING WORKS ===

Spinach, parsley, and mixed greens as the canonical trio, but any greens work. Chop in a food processor before folding in — food-processed greens distribute through the sauce evenly rather than sitting as leafy strands, which is what makes the sauce read cohesive rather than salad-y.

=== CREAM AS NEEDED FOR A REAL SAUCE ===

How much cream depends on how the ricotta + greens land — sometimes the mixture is already spreadable, sometimes it needs real thinning. Add enough cream to bring it to a sauce consistency that will coat the pasta once you toss with pasta water. Not a fixed amount; go by feel.

=== PASTA WATER TO LOOSEN AT THE END ===

Reserve pasta water before draining. Add enough to the finished sauce to bring it to the right coating consistency after the pasta goes in. Standard italian pasta-sauce move — the starchy water helps the sauce cling.

=== SIBLING — VEGAN SPINACH RICOTTA ===

See vegan-spinach-ricotta for the vegan analog. Different structure: that recipe is a raw blended base (cashews + tofu + spinach + basil + miso + nutritional yeast) used as a FILLING in downstream dishes (lasagna, calzones, stuffed shells) or thinned as a cold-ish pasta sauce. It's not a cooked skillet sauce like THIS recipe is. The vegan version's variant B borrows this recipe's seasoning register (nutmeg + red chili flakes + lemon zest/juice + porcini) but the underlying technique is raw-blend vs sear-and-fold.
